common_name: Veinte Cohol Banana (Twenty Cohol, Short-Cycle Cold-Hardy Fruiting Banana)

planting.note: Plant pups after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; its unusually short cycle lets it bloom and finish a bunch within a single growing season even at the cooler northern edge of banana country.

directions: Veinte Cohol is a short-statured, fast-fruiting banana that has drawn interest from coastal Georgia growers as a specialty crop because it reaches flowering and produces a mature bunch much faster than typical dessert bananas, sometimes within a single frost-free season from a spring-planted pup. The rhizome tolerates cooler conditions than tender Cavendish types, dying back at freezing but regrowing from the root system the following spring in zone 8b-9 gardens. Bunches are smaller than commercial Cavendish bunches, with plump, soft-textured fruit that trials have described as having a mild lemony note. Its compact height and shortened cropping cycle make it a practical choice for growers wanting homegrown bananas outside true tropical zones.

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost danger passes in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; the ABB cooking-type foliage tolerates wind and dry spells better than thin-leafed dessert Cavendish types.

directions: Cardava, also spelled Cardaba, is one of the most economically important banana cultivars of the Philippines, closely related to and often confused with Saba but classified as its own distinct ABB-group selection. It is grown primarily as a starchy cooking banana, harvested green and fried, boiled, or processed into chips, though it can also be eaten ripe. The tough, weather-resistant ABB foliage handles wind and drought better than dessert-type bananas, and the plant forms a large, vigorous clump over time. Give it full sun, deep rich soil, and heavy irrigation through the growing season, and expect over a year to first harvest.
sources: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development

common_name: Double Mahoi Banana (Dwarf Hawaiian Double-Bunching Banana)

planting.note: Plant after frost danger in a large container or warm bed; its compact size makes overwintering indoors in a bright spot practical outside zone 9b-11.

directions: Double Mahoi is a Hawaiian-origin sport of Dwarf Cavendish notable for an unusual trait: a single pseudostem can push out two flowering heads and mature two full bunches instead of the normal one, a rare habit in edible bananas. The fruit is a sweet, creamy Cavendish-type dessert banana, and the plant's compact stature makes it well suited to patios and large containers. It has no meaningful cold hardiness, so the pseudostem must be protected from frost, and it is best treated as a container specimen moved under cover before temperatures drop into the 40s. Give it full sun, rich soil, and heavy summer feeding to support its doubled fruit load.

common_name: Dwarf Namwah Banana (Compact Pisang Awak Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; its shorter stature suits smaller gardens and large containers better than standard Namwah.

directions: Dwarf Namwah is a compact selection of the Pisang Awak (Namwah) group, retaining the parent cultivar's sweet, creamy, slightly tangy fruit and good cold and disease tolerance while topping out at a much more manageable height. Like standard Namwah, the ABB genome contributes resilience against common Gulf South banana diseases and better cold tolerance than pure dessert-type Cavendish cultivars, with the pseudostem dying back in hard freezes and regrowing reliably from the rhizome. Its shorter size makes it easier to protect fully during winter and a better fit for smaller yards or large patio containers. Feed heavily and water consistently through the growing season for best bunch fill.

planting.note: Plant pups after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil in a wind-sheltered full-sun spot; the compact habit suits smaller gardens and greenhouse culture better than the full-size Brazilian.

directions: Dwarf Brazilian is a naturally occurring dwarf mutant of the Brazilian (Santa Catarina Prata) banana, imported to the United States in the late 1970s and valued for combining good cold and wind tolerance with a much shorter, sturdier pseudostem than its parent. It produces smaller but still sweet, good-flavored fruit, and the compact habit and strong wind resistance make it a practical choice for exposed Gulf Coast sites where taller cultivars are prone to leaf shredding or toppling. It tolerates cooler conditions better than tender dessert-type Cavendish bananas, though the pseudostem is still killed by a hard freeze and regrows from the rhizome in spring. Grow in full sun with rich, moist soil and heavy summer feeding.

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost passes in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; its tall, slender habit benefits from a wind-sheltered site.

directions: Ney Poovan is a diploid AB-genome dessert banana grown widely across India, prized for consistently high sweetness and a distinctive thin, sometimes lemon-yellow skin. It is one of the few edible banana groups to carry a wild Musa balbisiana contribution alongside acuminata parentage, giving it somewhat tougher foliage than pure AA or AAA dessert types. The plant grows tall and slender with a fairly long cycle to first bunch, so it rewards a full frost-free season, rich soil, and steady irrigation and feeding. It has no significant cold tolerance and should be treated as a warm-season specialty planting in zone 9 and sheltered from wind given its height.

planting.note: Plant divisions or pups after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from wind.

directions: FHIA-18 is a hybrid banana bred by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research (FHIA), derived in part from the cold- and wind-tolerant Dwarf Brazilian cultivar, and selected for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf spot and Fusarium wilt (Panama disease). The fruit ripens naturally to yellow with a sweet, mild apple-like flavor reminiscent of its Gros Michel-type ancestry, but with a softer texture. It is a semi-dwarf, productive, disease-tolerant option for gardeners in humid Gulf South climates where Sigatoka pressure limits older commercial cultivars. Give it full sun, rich soil, and heavy summer feeding and irrigation to support a full bunch within one growing season.

common_name: Yangambi Km5 Banana (Nematode-Resistant Ibota Dessert Banana)

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost danger passes in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Yangambi Km5 is a traditional AAA-genome dessert banana of the Ibota subgroup, originally collected in the Democratic Republic of Congo, that has been widely studied by tropical agriculture researchers as a rare natural source of resistance to burrowing nematode and other root-damaging pests that plague most commercial banana cultivars. This underlying disease and pest tolerance can translate into a sturdier, lower-maintenance plant for home gardeners, though it remains fully cold-tender like other AAA dessert types and must be grown in a warm, frost-free season. The fruit is a sweet dessert banana suitable for fresh eating. Grow it in full sun with rich, consistently moist soil and heavy feeding through the warm months.

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost danger passes in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake the stalk as bunches fill out since fruit is long and heavy.

directions: Nendran is one of the most widely grown AAB-genome bananas of Kerala, India, valued as a true dual-purpose cultivar: the long, thick, slightly curved fruit is cooked as a starchy vegetable, notably fried into chips, when green and eaten as a sweet dessert banana when fully ripe. It grows into a tall, vigorous, wind-resistant plant and needs deep fertile soil and generous irrigation to fill out its characteristically large, elongated fruit. It has no notable cold tolerance and should be reserved for the warmest, most sheltered parts of a zone 9b-11 garden. Feed heavily through the growing season, since it is a heavier feeder than many dessert-type bananas.

common_name: Formosana Banana (GCTCV-218, Fusarium Wilt-Resistant Cavendish Somaclone)

planting.note: Plant tissue-culture plantlets or pups after frost danger passes in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Formosana, registered from the research line GCTCV-218, is a Giant Cavendish somaclonal variant selected by the Taiwan Banana Research Institute after a farmer noticed it surviving in Fusarium wilt (Panama disease)-infested soil that killed neighboring plants. It has since been adopted in Taiwan, the Philippines, and Mozambique as a Cavendish-type replacement in ground contaminated with the aggressive tropical race 4 strain of the fungus. The fruit is a standard sweet, mild Cavendish-type dessert banana, and the plant otherwise behaves like other AAA Cavendish types, with no particular cold hardiness and susceptibility to pseudostem freeze damage. Its main value for a home garden is peace of mind in soil with a history of banana wilt problems; grow it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and heavy feeding.
